scope: Eight original additive case studies in art direction, embodied interaction and portable/networked production; no canonical or source-language bodies overwritten.

entries.title: The people inside the pixels
entries.event_semantics: Final Fantasy III's 1990 release anchors this study of work across the first and third games. Shibuya's 2013 and Ishii's 2020 interviews are retrospective accounts with distinct responsibilities, not a single uniform production pipeline.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers, translators and institutions credited per card.
body: Kazuko Shibuya remembers making the first Final Fantasy's opening landscape under a severe memory limit. A complete new picture would not fit. Hills and sea reused small graphic elements, sometimes flipped to vary their appearance, while the foreground became a black silhouette. The solution kept the travelers readable without supplying every surface with new detail. In her 2013 account, the memorable image grew from choices about what to repeat and what to leave empty, rather than from an unrestricted illustration reduced to screen size.

Shibuya also corrects an appealingly simple account of the game's artwork. Yoshitaka Amano's illustrations did not supply every playable character in a straightforward sequence of adaptations. The internal team created its characters, and some monsters came from Amano's monochrome drawings. Limited available colours required further decisions when those monsters reached the screen; other designers, including Shibuya herself, created monsters too. Her account identifies several kinds of authorship inside one visual style. The person supplying an illustration and the person choosing its pixels were not interchangeable credits.

Koichi Ishii describes another route into the same craft. During the first Final Fantasy, Shibuya was occupied with Rad Racer, so he asked Takashi Tokita to teach him the sprite tools. His first attempt disappeared because he saved it incorrectly. Eventually a working side-view battle display persuaded Hironobu Sakaguchi to use that approach for the characters. Ishii recalls continuing to adjust individual pixels himself. Planning a character, learning a tool and judging an animated result happened together, rather than as neatly separated departments.

For Final Fantasy III, Ishii wanted each job to have its own pose and imagined background. A small palette made those differences difficult. Instead of always reserving one colour for skin, he experimented with bright yellow, khaki and blue to find another family of characters. For the first game, he describes arranging black marks in white mountains for the colour effects produced by a CRT television. The intended picture included the display's behaviour. A sharp modern view can therefore show different relationships from the image these artists were composing.

entries.title: Drawing a rival for Sonic
entries.event_semantics: Sonic CD's 1993 artwork is the selected case within the broader Sonic Team commission. Hoshino's 2011 and 2013 recollections are separate publications; the first Sonic game's Naka/Ohshima/Yasuhara history remains in the existing parent.
entries.summary: A machine needs its own movement.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers, translators and institutions credited per card.
body: Sonic CD needed a visual identity that would distinguish the new disc game from its cartridge relatives. Artist Kazuyuki Hoshino recalls being fascinated by the polished, metallic appearance then associated with computer graphics. For the title animation, the team photographed a Sonic figurine with a Polaroid camera, scanned the pictures and used them as a starting point. The metallic emblem added contrast around the character. What appears to announce a new technological age also contains a practical studio procedure involving a physical object and still photographs.

Metal Sonic began with a clear relationship: an opponent who could stand beside Sonic as his double and rival. Hoshino describes imagining the red iris inside a dark eye, then designing for a direct contest between the characters. Simply repeating Sonic's movement seemed insufficient. A robot allowed another answer, and the imagined force of a drag racer's launch suggested the large booster on its back. The machine's appearance expressed a different source of speed before the race itself demonstrated what that difference could do.

In a separate 2013 interview, Hoshino explains character drawing through the actions a game requires. Sonic's spiked ball presents the protective, attacking shape used while jumping; visual design communicates an interaction rather than merely decorating it. Hoshino also distinguishes his own central intention from the feedback sought elsewhere in Sega, including Europe and marketing. That wider consultation had become more formal than in the early days. A recognizable character could emerge from a designer's proposal while still being examined by colleagues with different responsibilities.

Hoshino identifies another change when characters move from flat images into three dimensions. A two-dimensional game can repeatedly show a figure from its most effective angles. A three-dimensional model must also work from behind and from views the earlier sprite never exposed. The task is not finished by copying a familiar face. Parts that once remained unseen need decisions of their own. His explanation makes the adaptation a problem of sustained readability around a body, with the original appeal tested against a much larger range of viewpoints.

entries.title: An illustration enters another world
entries.event_semantics: Final Fantasy III's 1990 artwork anchors this case. The translated 1990 testimony has an unidentified original publication, disclosed in source metadata; the second firsthand interview is dated 24 June 2024. Neither source makes Amano the sole author of in-game sprites.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers, translators and institutions credited per card.
body: Working for a game did not give Yoshitaka Amano one distant deadline and a blank year. In testimony dated 1990, he describes Final Fantasy III alongside his other illustration commitments. Monsters and concept pictures were needed at different stages, keeping the project in mind throughout development. His drawings were not inserted directly as screen graphics. He was interested in seeing what happened when others translated them into the game. The image players encountered was therefore one result of a longer exchange between different kinds of work.

For earlier Final Fantasy monsters, Amano recalls producing monochrome ink drawings. With the third game, he began with colour instead, finding that the change generated ideas during the act of drawing. A separate decision shaped its cover: Square requested a figure holding two blades, replacing his initial thought of a landscape without people. He came to prefer the stronger impact of that figure. The account places colour, composition and a client's request inside the process, rather than presenting a finished illustration as a solitary, inevitable inspiration.

In a 2024 interview, Amano traces Square's invitation to his covers and illustrations for fantasy novels. He describes working from written descriptions while looking for colours appropriate to a character's personality and role. Fantasy allowed him to draw subjects that need not exist. Yet the game project also supplied collaborators and expectations. He remembers being corrected when he first tried drawing pixel art. Joining that production meant discovering where his particular approach could contribute, rather than simply reproducing the same craft in another format.

The same interview accompanies clothing that places Amano's drawings beside familiar pixel characters. He enjoys the difference: an image can change character depending on which side of a garment someone sees. His studio contains pencils, crayons and paints, and he remarks on the different expressions those materials allow. These are specific objects and processes, not evidence that the illustrations and game graphics have identical authorship. Keeping both visible lets the player recognize a relationship without flattening the drawing, its adaptation and its later public life into one image.

entries.title: The marks left on purpose
entries.event_semantics: MGS2's 2001 production is the historical anchor. Konami's companion-artbook interview is undated on its surviving page and discusses completed promotional illustrations; the separate Left Alive interview is 11 February 2019. Specific 2019 collaboration details are not reassigned to the MGS2 team.
entries.summary: Shinkawa works between paper and motion.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers, translators and institutions credited per card.
body: Yoji Shinkawa's companion interview for The Art of Metal Gear Solid 2 treats the illustrations as working objects with different purposes. A Raiden picture introduced the character in presentation material for collaborators, while other drawings served magazines or packaging. Discussing white gaps in his images, he explains leaving something for the viewer to imagine. The unfinished space is deliberate rather than a missing production step. A drawing can establish a character through selected marks without describing every surface that a modeler might later need to build.

The roughness in another Raiden image did not come solely from a digital filter. Shinkawa describes drawing with thin ink, making a black-and-white photocopy and scanning that rougher version instead of the original. The intermediate copy changed the texture before further digital work. A different illustration used Photoshop's brush directly when time was short. These examples resist a simple division between traditional and computer art. Paper, copying and software were successive tools whose visible effects could be chosen to suit a particular image and deadline.

For Left Alive, Shinkawa received brief profiles for three central characters, then began with rough versions of Leonid. In his 2019 account, the design developed through checking the direction and balance of the cast. Producer Shinji Hashimoto and director Toshifumi Nabeshima supplied feedback through several rounds. The recognizable hand was working inside a conversation about the game's people. Revisions were neither an erasure of authorship nor a guarantee that every sketch would survive: they were how a supplied character profile became an agreed production design.

A design could also change after a character began moving. Shinkawa explains that equipment placement and small visual features sometimes produced problems only in the game, leading to discussions and adjustments with the production team. He reviewed models and motion as well as supplying drawings. His usual toolkit still included ordinary copy paper, pencil and brush pen, followed by scanning and Photoshop. The process returned repeatedly from image to modeled body. Finishing a compelling sheet of artwork did not remove the need to examine what happened on screen.

entries.title: A gesture enters the room
entries.event_semantics: The original Wii Sports and Wii's 2006 launch anchor the story. The US strap replacement notice is dated 15 December 2006 and concerns about 2 million straps in that programme, not a worldwide console recall or a general measure of accessibility.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers, translators and institutions credited per card.
body: Wii Sports began among experiments made to test possible controllers. Tennis director Keizo Ota recalls receiving different hardware proposals and quickly building software around them. The remote's rod-like shape suggested a racket. The process also ran in reverse: a working game gave the hardware team something concrete to examine. Producer Katsuya Eguchi later had to turn these scattered prototypes into a coherent collection. The gesture did not arrive first as a finished instruction for a finished machine. Its usefulness became visible while people tried competing proposals together.

The audience mattered beyond the person holding the remote. During demonstrations, director Takayuki Shimamura noticed spectators advising baseball players about their swings, although conventional sporting form was not itself a required control input. Ota imagined relatives and friends who did not normally play games trying Tennis. These are the developers' observations and hopes, not a measurement that everyone could participate. Their design question expanded from whether the action worked to whether someone else in the room could recognize it, discuss it and want a turn.

Moving the controller gave a small physical component new importance. A December 2006 US notice records Nintendo's wrist-strap replacement programme after cords broke when players used excessive force and accidentally released the remote. It reports three minor injuries not requiring medical attention, all during Wii Sports. The affected programme covered about two million straps. The same gesture intended to make play immediately understandable had to coexist with hands, furniture and people nearby. The accessory was part of that interaction, not simply packaging around it.

The replacement changed the cord from 0.6 millimetres to 1.0 millimetre in diameter. Nintendo arranged for consumers to obtain the revised strap, while the notice distinguished the dates after which console packages and separately sold remotes should include it. This was a material revision to an object already circulating in homes. Reading it beside the software team's interviews reveals two scales of design work: deciding what a swing could mean on screen, and revising a small connection that helped keep the physical remote attached to its player.

entries.title: Combat within reach of the hands
entries.event_semantics: Halo Combat Evolved's 2001 Xbox version anchors the shipped controls. The Griesemer interview explicitly says originally posted 10 May 2000 despite its migrated 2001 header; its design intentions predate the final Xbox product and are labelled accordingly. Accessible here means approachable interaction, not a disability-accessibility certification.
entries.summary: A shooter offers choices beyond aim.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers, translators and institutions credited per card.
body: Before Halo reached Xbox, designer Jaime Griesemer described a game in which immediate decisions should matter alongside accurate shooting. Adding another strategic objective was not, by itself, enough: movement and small tactical choices had to change an encounter. His early interview describes an intention rather than a complete record of the finished game. It is useful because it places the designer's attention on what happens between shots. The player needs meaningful actions to choose, not only a demanding target to keep under a cursor.

Griesemer applied that reasoning to cooperation too. Talking about a plan, he argued, was less rewarding than actually carrying it out with another player. He wanted cooperative actions to become natural enough that constant explanation was unnecessary, while still providing communication tools. The same interview treats a substantial single-player game as essential context rather than a practice arena for multiplayer. These priorities connect the moment-to-moment encounter with the world around it. A shared action should be understandable through what people are doing, not only through instructions they exchange.

The original Xbox manual gives those decisions a physical arrangement. One thumbstick moves the player and the other turns and aims; the triggers separate firing from throwing a grenade. Melee and weapon switching have their own buttons rather than requiring a journey through a long inventory. The arrangement lets an encounter change without making the player change devices or stop controlling the camera. Learning the pad still takes practice. The important relationship is that movement, looking and several kinds of response can remain available together.

Information on the visor gives those responses a rhythm. The manual distinguishes health, which does not return automatically, from a shield that recharges when damage stops. Direction indicators locate incoming fire, and the motion tracker shows movement rather than supplying an all-seeing map of every enemy. Pausing behind cover can therefore restore one resource while leaving another depleted. The screen is not merely reporting a score after the fact: it offers signals for deciding whether to continue, withdraw, search for help or approach from another direction.

entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers, translators and institutions credited per card.
body: Phantasy Star Online did not begin as a story waiting for a network connection. In a Sega.com interview, Yuji Naka says the team experimented with an online game for Dreamcast's modem, then chose Phantasy Star's setting. ChuChu Rocket had also served as a practical step toward understanding online play. The order matters: technical experiments preceded the finished fictional frame. Bringing a console into that space required work below the game itself, including the different networking arrangements players encountered in different countries.

Even agreeing when to meet became a production question. PSO displayed Swatch's internet-time system, but Naka explains that the value came from the server rather than simply trusting the Dreamcast's own clock. Servers in different time zones had to agree, and a player's incorrectly set console time could not become the common reference. This modest display depended on coordination beyond the room. The online interface was carrying a practical promise: players entering through different local machines should still be able to refer to the same time.

The original manual turns another social problem into a small object: the Guild Card. A player could send one to someone met online, keep received cards and search for that person's current location later. If the person was online, Simple Mail provided a message; a result in a visual lobby could offer a way to meet there. The dungeon group was therefore not the only unit of memory. The game supplied a route from a temporary encounter to the possibility of finding that particular player again.

Ending the session also had explicit rules. The manual directs players to Quit Game to disconnect and save, rather than treating power-off as an equivalent departure. It distinguishes the main save from the Guild Card file and warns about lost items or money after an improper exit or disconnection. An optional inactivity timer could save and disconnect after a chosen interval. These procedures made character persistence understandable, but also exposed its limits. Leaving the shared space was part of using it, not simply the absence of play.

entries.title: The library travels with the machine
entries.event_semantics: Steam Deck's 2022 first generation anchors the feature. Valve's August 2022 book and launch-era Steamworks FAQ are historical evidence, not promises that every Windows game, control configuration or current hardware variant behaves identically.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers, translators and institutions credited per card.
body: Valve's 2022 Steam Deck book traces the idea back to work on the Steam Controller roughly a decade earlier. The team wanted demanding PC games in a handheld but did not yet have the necessary battery-sized hardware budget. Prototypes could explore the form while that constraint remained. Later, work with AMD on a custom processor brought the design closer to production. During the pandemic, colleagues shipped prototypes between one another to test ergonomics and control positions. The machine emerged through repeated handling as well as a component specification.

The book also describes earlier products as parts of the handheld's preparation. Steam Controller work supplied Steam Input; Steam Link contributed streaming and networking experience; Steam Machines exposed operating-system and Windows-to-Linux problems that helped lead to Proton. These projects did not need to share the same physical shape to contribute to Deck. They supplied tools for an existing library whose games expected many different environments. The historical question is therefore larger than which processor could fit: the software relationships had to become portable too.

Valve's launch-era developer questions make that variety concrete. A game built around a cursor may need hovering, different mouse buttons or precise movement, so a touchscreen alone is not always the right translation. The FAQ recommends considering the trackpads, and describes combining gyroscope aiming with a stick or pad. Developers can offer both conventional and motion configurations through Steam Input. The controls offer alternatives rather than one compulsory gesture. Bringing a PC game to the hand also means examining which assumptions its original interface made.

Testing did not require a secret version of the machine. Valve states that a retail Steam Deck can serve as a development kit using the same tools and methods. The FAQ also describes checking controller support, legibility, performance and system compatibility for Deck Verified. A library entry is thus accompanied by a practical review of how it behaves on that device. The category is not a promise that every game will work: it makes some of the adaptation visible before the player chooses what to install.
